sections.title: Verb tense in the reported clause
sections.content:
When we report something that was said or thought in the past, we often use a past tense in the reported clause:
• Yusuf said that he didn't want anything to eat.
If the original situation was already in the past, we often use the past perfect:
• Police said that they had found the missing girl.

sections.title: Permanent or habitual situations
sections.content:
When the situation described is a permanent / habitual situation, we can use either a present or past tense if the reporting verb is in the past:
• She argued that Carl is / was the best person for the job.
We prefer a past tense if we are not sure what we are reporting is true:
• Yasemin told me that she had two houses. (suggests either that this is perhaps not true, or that she no longer has them)

sections.title: Verb tense in the reporting clause
sections.content:
We can use a present tense for the reporting verb when we report current news, opinions, or information that we have heard but don't know if it's true:
• I hear you’re unhappy with your job.
• The law says that no one under the age of 16 can buy a lottery ticket.
Using a present tense reporting verb emphasises that what was said is still true or relevant.

exercises.question: 'I've never been in love with Oliver.' → She ___ that she ___ in love with Oliver.
exercises.hint: Use past perfect or past simple in the that-clause after denied.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: denied / had ever been (or was)
Use past perfect or past simple in the that-clause after denied.

exercises.sentence: She told the interviewer that she studies French at university.
exercises.correction: She told the interviewer that she studied French at university.
exercises.hint: In reported speech, present simple → past simple (tense backshift).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: she studied French at university
In reported speech, tenses shift back one step: present simple ('studies') → past simple ('studied'). The past perfect ('had studied') is also possible and emphasises that the studying was completed before the moment of speaking. Both are correct.

exercises.question: 'I think the vase is around 250 years old.' → She ___ that the vase ___ around 250 years old.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: estimated / was (or had been)
We use the past perfect here because this action happened before another past event.
💡 Reporting a past thought.

exercises.sentence: He said me that he will call me the next morning.
exercises.correction: He told me that he would call me the next morning.
acceptable: He told me that he would call
He said that he would call me
exercises.hint: Two errors: 'said me' → 'told me'; 'will' → 'would' (backshift from future to conditional).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: He told me that he would call me the next morning
Two errors to fix: (1) 'said me' → 'told me' ('tell' needs a personal object; 'say' does not). (2) 'will' → 'would' (tense backshift in reported speech: will shifts to would). Also note: 'tomorrow' → 'the next morning/day' in reported speech.

exercises.question: Engineers hope that they ___ the problems with the bridge now that new supports have been built.
exercises.hint: Present perfect continuous/simple after 'hope' for present relevance.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: have solved (or solve)
Present perfect continuous/simple after 'hope' for present relevance. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.sentence: The current policy states that all employees must declared their expenses monthly.
exercises.correction: The current policy states that all employees must declare their expenses monthly.
exercises.hint: After 'must', always use the bare infinitive — no '-ed' ending.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must declare
After all modal verbs (must, should, can, could, may, might, will, would), use the bare infinitive (no -s, -ed, or -ing). 'Must declared' incorrectly applies a past tense ending to the infinitive. Note: present tense reporting verbs ('states', 'says') do not trigger tense backshift.

exercises.question: The current law ___ that an employee has the right to appeal.
exercises.hint: Laws usually use present tense reporting verbs.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: states
Laws usually use present tense reporting verbs.

exercises.question: Protesting that he ___ at home all day. (Nokes)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was / had been
We use the past perfect here because this action happened before another past event.
💡 Nokes' past situation reported.

exercises.question: Reminded Barnes that he ___ entitled to have a lawyer present.
exercises.hint: Past reporting verb usually leads to a past reported verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was
Past reporting verb usually leads to a past reported verb.
